practical.title: File I/O and Command-Line Arguments — Intensive Lab
practical.sourceActivity: File I/O and Command-Line Arguments — Intensive Lab

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Run the baseline file-copy program
teachingPlaylist.description: Compile and run the provided C program to copy source.txt to a destination. Observe how argc/argv and fopen are used.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: See a working example connecting argv to fopen and the copy loop.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We'll compile the supplied program and run it with two filenames. Watch the usage check run if you call it wrong. After copying, open the destination file to compare contents with the source.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: gcc copy_file.c -o copy_file; ./copy_file source.txt destination.txt; cat destination.txt
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You have a text file source.txt and want to create a copy quickly from the terminal without opening an editor.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Predict what the program prints and what destination.txt will contain. Then run the commands and compare.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Not checking argc and then indexing argv when it's missing can crash the program.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You saw argument parsing, fopen checks, a fgetc/fputc loop, and closing files. The destination file matched the source.
codeSteps: Open copy_file.c and read main signature to find argc and argv usage.
Open destination.txt with cat to verify content.

teachingPlaylist.title: Make the program binary-safe
teachingPlaylist.description: Change fopen modes from "r"/"w" to "rb"/"wb" so copying preserves bytes on all platforms.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand text vs binary file modes and the minimal change to make copying robust.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Edit the two fopen lines to use rb and wb. Recompile and run; behavior for text files will be the same, but binary data will now be preserved.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Change input_file = fopen(input_filename, "r"); to input_file = fopen(input_filename, "rb"); and output_file = fopen(output_filename, "w"); to output_file = fopen(output_filename, "wb");
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You need to copy an image file where newline translation would corrupt the output if text mode were used.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Make the two edits, recompile, and copy the same source file. Observe whether destination content still matches source.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Changing only one of the modes might still leave transformations on some platforms.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Binary mode preserves bytes byte-for-byte. This small edit improves portability.
codeSteps: Locate the fopen calls in copy_file.c.
Save, compile, and run with the same filenames.
Verify the destination file contents match the source.

teachingPlaylist.title: Add a byte counter and print progress
teachingPlaylist.description: Introduce a counter to the copy loop so the program reports how many bytes were copied.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Learn how to augment an existing loop with a counter to produce runtime metrics.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Declare a long count = 0; before the copy loop, increment it for each character copied, and print the total after copying. Use wc -c to confirm the count.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Add long count = 0; then inside loop: fputc(c, output_file); count++; After loop: printf("%ld bytes copied.\n", count);
teachingPlaylist.scenario: When copying large files you want an audit line to confirm how many bytes were processed.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Implement the counter, compile, run, and confirm the printed number matches wc -c output.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Using int for very large files may overflow; prefer long or size_t for counts.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Counters are simple, effective diagnostics that make testing and logging easier.
codeSteps: Add long count = 0; near the variable declarations.
Inside the copy loop add count++; after fputc.
After fclose calls, print the count with printf("%ld bytes copied.\n", count).

teachingPlaylist.title: Verify edge cases and design an overwrite-avoidance plan
teachingPlaylist.description: Test missing-argument and missing-file behavior. Design a backup/ refusal strategy for when the output file exists.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand and test expected error messages and think through a safe extension to avoid accidental data loss.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Run without arguments to see the Usage message. Run with a missing input file to see an error. Then outline code to detect existing output files and either create a .bak or refuse to overwrite.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: ./copy_file -> shows Usage; ./copy_file missing.txt dest.txt -> Error: Could not open input file 'missing.txt'.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You run a copy tool in a script; an accidental overwrite could destroy data, so adding safety checks is important.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Try the two commands above and then write pseudocode to implement a -b flag that backs up existing outputs.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Assuming the output file will always open; permissions or directory issues can prevent opening for writing.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Good programs handle wrong usage and missing files gracefully; preventing overwrites is a common and important extension.
codeSteps: Run ./copy_file missing.txt dest.txt to confirm input error.
Sketch pseudocode to check if output exists and rename it before opening for writing.
Implement the -b flag in a future change if desired.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand: Run the baseline copy program
tasks.narratorGuide: We're starting by running the provided C program exactly as given. Read these lines aloud: int main open parenthesis int argc comma char star argv open bracket close bracket. Notice the usage check if argc is not three. That protects us from accessing argv out of bounds. We'll compile with gcc, run the program with source.txt and destination.txt, and then open destination.txt to confirm the copy. While the program runs, watch for the printed success message. Prediction time: do you expect the destination file to contain the same lines and newline characters? Pause, then run the commands and compare. Good — that observation links the code to real files on disk.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment: Make the program binary-safe
tasks.narratorGuide: Now you will make a tiny but important change. Open copy_file.c and find the two fopen calls — one uses "r" and the other uses "w". Replace them with "rb" and "wb" respectively. This specific change makes the program safe when copying binary files. On POSIX systems you won't see a difference for our text file, but the intent matters and the code will behave correctly on Windows. After you save, run gcc copy_file.c -o copy_file and then run ./copy_file source.txt destination.txt. Expect the same success message. Good — you just performed a surgical edit that improves robustness.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate: Add a byte counter to report how many bytes were copied
tasks.narratorGuide: Time to add a small, useful feature: a byte counter. Open copy_file.c and add a declaration: long count = 0; just after the int c comment. Inside the copy loop, after fputc(c, output_file); add count++;. After closing the files, add printf("%ld bytes copied.\n", count); — or augment the existing success message. Save, compile, and run. You'll see both the success message and the number of bytes copied. This gives immediate measurable feedback and is helpful when testing with unknown file sizes.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend: Test edge cases and plan an extension
tasks.narratorGuide: Now we verify behaviors you must handle in real programs: wrong usage and missing files. Run the program without arguments: ./copy_file — the program should print a Usage message including argv[0]. Next, try copying a non-existent file: ./copy_file missing.txt new.txt. You should see a clear error: Could not open input file 'missing.txt'. These checks force you to think about user errors. Extension challenge: design code to detect if the output file already exists; either refuse to overwrite, prompt the user, or rename the existing file to a .bak. Pause and write one-sentence pseudocode for that extension before moving on.
